column2: By a wondrous method and by divine contrivance, O Bharata, the hard-to-see king, mace in hand, lay within the water, beyond the power of any man to find.
Then King Duryodhana, dwelling within the water, heard a tumultuous sound like the roar of clouds.
Yudhishthira, O king of kings, came with his brothers to that lake, O great king, for the slaying of your sons.
With the blare of conches and the rumble of chariot-wheels, raising great clouds of dust and shaking the earth,
the great chariot-warriors Kritavarman, Kripa and Drona's son, hearing the noise of Yudhishthira's army, said this to the king:
Here come the Pandavas, delighted and victorious; let us withdraw for now, if you permit us.
Hearing those renowned men, Duryodhana said "So be it," and, lord, held the lake still by his illusion.
Having taken leave of the king, deeply sunk in grief, Kripa and the other chariot-warriors went far away, O great king.
Having gone a long way, they saw a banyan tree, O revered one, and sat down there, greatly weary, thinking of the king.

The mighty son of Dhritarashtra lies asleep, holding back the water, and the Pandavas, wishing for battle, have also reached that place.
mahabharata:9:29.65	How will the battle be? How will the king fare? How, O king, will the Pandavas deal with the Kaurava?
Thus thinking, O king, Kripa and the other chariot-warriors unyoked their horses from the chariots and made camp there.
Reaching Lake Dvaipayana, O best of the Kurus, and seeing it held still by Dhritarashtra's son, the water-bed closed, the delight of the Kurus spoke these words to Vasudeva.

Look at this illusion that Dhritarashtra's son has worked in the water: he lies holding back the water, with no fear of any man.
mahabharata:9:30.4	Having made this divine illusion, he has gone into the water; this crafty-minded one will not escape with his life by his trickery.
mahabharata:9:30.5	Even if the wielder of the thunderbolt himself aids him in the battle, yet, Madhava, the world will see him slain in the fight.
[Vasudeva said:] "Destroy this illusion of the illusionist by illusion, Bharata; the illusionist must be slain by illusion—this is true, Yudhishthira.
Using many devices and means, working illusion upon the water, slay, O best of the Bharatas, the sinful Suyodhana.
By devices and means Indra slew the Daityas and Danavas; by many such means the great-souled one bound Bali.
By devices and means in former times the great asura Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu were slain, and Vritra too was slain, O king, by contrivance, without doubt.
So too the Rakshasa Ravana, son of Pulastya's line, was slain by Rama with his kin and followers, O king; resorting to contrivance, you too must show your valour.
By devices and means, O king, in ancient times I slew the great Daitya Taraka and the mighty Viprachitti,
Vatapi and Ilvala, and Trishiras too, O lord; the asuras Sunda and Upasunda were slain by contrivance alone.
By devices and means Indra enjoys heaven, O lord; contrivance is powerful, O king, Yudhishthira; nothing else is.
Daityas, Danavas, Rakshasas and kings were slain by devices and means; therefore practise contrivance."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed by Vasudeva, the Pandava of keen vows, the son of Kunti, smiling as it were, spoke to your son lying in the water, O great king.

Suyodhana, why have you undertaken this venture in the water, having destroyed all the kshatriyas and your own family, O lord of men?
mahabharata:9:30.17	Having entered the lake today, wishing to save your life—rise, O king, and fight with us, Suyodhana.
mahabharata:9:30.18	Where has that pride gone, best of men, and where that honour, that you stand fearful, O king, having stilled the water?
mahabharata:9:30.19	All people in the assembly call you a hero, but I think your heroism is vain, lying in the water.
mahabharata:9:30.20	Rise, O king, and fight; you are a kshatriya born of a noble family, a Kaurava especially; remember your birth.
mahabharata:9:30.21	How, praising your birth in the Kuru line, do you enter the water out of fear of battle and stay there?
mahabharata:9:30.22	Refusing battle and holding no ground is not the eternal dharma; flight from the field, O king, is ignoble and does not lead to heaven.
mahabharata:9:30.23	How, wishing to live, without reaching the far shore of battle, having seen these sons, brothers and fathers fallen,
mahabharata:9:30.24	your kinsmen, friends, maternal uncles and relatives—having had them slain, dear one, how do you stay in a lake now?
mahabharata:9:30.25	You think yourself a hero but are no hero; you speak falsely, Bharata, saying 'I am a hero,' ill-minded one, in the hearing of all the world.
mahabharata:9:30.26	Heroes never flee at the sight of enemies; or say, hero, by what resolve you abandon the fight.
mahabharata:9:30.27	So rise and fight, casting off your fear, Suyodhana, having had all your army and brothers slain.
mahabharata:9:30.28	Now is no time to set your mind on life, wishing for dharma, for one like you, Suyodhana, having resorted to the kshatriya's duty,
mahabharata:9:30.29	who, relying on Karna and on Shakuni, son of Subala, did not understand yourself, as though immortal, through delusion.
mahabharata:9:30.30	Having done that very great sin, fight back, Bharata; how can one like you through delusion choose flight?
mahabharata:9:30.31	Where has your manliness gone, and where your pride, Suyodhana? Where your prowess, and where your great bluster?
mahabharata:9:30.32	Where has your skill in weapons gone, that you lie in a lake? Rise and fight, Bharata—do not abandon a kshatriya's duty.
mahabharata:9:30.33	Either conquer us and rule this earth, or, slain by us, you will sleep on the ground, Bharata.
mahabharata:9:30.34	This is the first duty ordained by the great-souled Creator; follow it rightly, great chariot-warrior, and be king.
[Duryodhana said:] "It is no wonder, great king, that fear enters a living being; and I have not fled from fear of death, Bharata.
Without chariot, without quiver, my rear charioteer slain, alone and without followers in the battle, I wished for rest.
Not for the sake of life, nor from fear, nor from despondency, lord of men, have I entered this water; I did it out of weariness.
You too take rest, son of Kunti, and those who follow you; rising, I shall fight you all in battle."
[Yudhishthira said:] "We are all rested, and have long been seeking you; so rise now and fight here, Suyodhana.
Either slaying the Parthas in battle, win a flourishing kingdom, or slain by us in the fight, attain the world of heroes."
[Duryodhana said:] "For whose sake I wanted the kingdom of the Kurus, O delight of the Kurus—those brothers of mine are all slain, lord of men.
I do not care to enjoy an earth whose jewels are gone and whose bull-like kshatriyas are slain, like a widowed woman.
Even today, Yudhishthira, I hope to conquer you, breaking the spirit of the Panchalas and Pandavas, bull of the Bharatas.
But now I think there is never any need for battle, with Drona and Karna dead and the grandsire slain.
Let this earth be yours alone now, O king; for what king, without allies, would wish to rule a kingdom?
Having lost such friends, sons, brothers and fathers, and with the kingdom taken by you, who like me would live?
I shall go to the forest, clad in deerskins; I have no delight in kingship, my side destroyed, Bharata.
With most of her kinsmen slain, her horses and elephants slain, this earth is yours, O king; enjoy her free of fever.
I shall go to the forest, wearing deerskin; I, defeated, have no longing for life today, lord.
Go and enjoy the earth, O king of kings, her lords slain, warriors slain, jewels lost and ramparts ruined, as you please."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Dear one, do not speak these lamentations from the water; I do not take them to heart, any more than the cry of a bird of prey.
Even if you were able to give, Suyodhana, I would not wish to rule the earth given by you.
I would not take unrighteously this earth given by you; for acceptance of gifts is not the dharma of a kshatriya, O king.
I do not want the whole earth given by you; rather, having conquered you in battle, I shall enjoy this earth.
And being no master of the earth, how can you wish to give it? Why did you not give this earth, O king, at that very time?
When we begged for the sake of dharma and for the peace of our family, you first refused the mighty Vrishni, O king.
Why do you give now? What confusion of mind is this? What king, when attacked, would wish to give the earth?
You are not now master to give the earth, delight of the Kurus, nor to seize it by force; how can you wish to give it? Conquer me in battle and rule this earth.
You did not give us earlier even as much land as could be held on the point of a needle.
How then do you give away this earth, lord of men? You who would not give up a needle's point before, how do you now give up the land?
Having attained such sovereignty and ruled this earth, what fool would resolve to give the earth to an enemy?
You, through sheer folly, bewildered, do not understand; though desiring to give the earth, you will be freed only by your life today.
Either conquer us and rule this earth, or, slain by us, go to the supreme worlds.
While both of us live, O king, there will surely be no certainty of victory for all creatures, in me and in you.
Your life, ill-minded one, now rests with me; I might let you live if I wished, but you are not fit to live.
You tried to burn us in particular, with venomous snakes and poison, by pushing us into water, and cheated us, O king, by seizing the kingdom.
For this reason your sinful life cannot remain; rise, rise and fight—that will be better for you."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus, lord of men, those heroes there again and again spoke various words, full of triumph.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Never before had he heard such threats; he was honoured by the whole world as a king.
And this entire earth, with its barbarians and forests, was upheld by his favour, as you saw directly, Sanjaya.
Thus threatened especially by the sons of Pandu, deprived of his own servants, surrounded in a lonely place,
having heard those harsh, triumphant words again and again, what did he say to the Pandavas? Tell me, Sanjaya."
[Sanjaya said:] When your son, lying in the water, was thus threatened, O king, by Yudhishthira with his brothers,
hearing those harsh words, the lord of men, in distress, sighed long and hot again and again from the water.
The king, within the water, wringing his hands again and again, set his mind on battle and said to the king:

You Parthas are all with your friends, with chariots and mounts; I am alone, hard-pressed, without chariot, my mounts slain.
mahabharata:9:31.10	Surrounded by many in chariots with weapons in hand, how can I, alone, on foot and weaponless, dare to fight?
mahabharata:9:31.11	Fight me one at a time, Yudhishthira; it is not proper for one to fight many heroes in battle,
mahabharata:9:31.12	especially one without armour, weary, resorting to water, with limbs sorely wounded and with mounts and soldiers exhausted.
mahabharata:9:31.13	I have no fear of you, O king, nor of Partha, nor of Vrikodara, Phalguna, Vasudeva, or the Panchalas,
mahabharata:9:31.14	nor of the twins, nor of Yuyudhana, nor of any of your other soldiers; though I am enraged, alone, I cannot here fight them all.
mahabharata:9:31.15	The fame of good men has dharma as its root, lord of men; protecting dharma and fame, I speak.
mahabharata:9:31.16	Rising, I shall fight you all in battle, all who have come in succession, as the year does the seasons.
mahabharata:9:31.17	Today, though weaponless and chariotless, I shall destroy you with your chariots and horses by my splendour, as the sun at the end of night does all the stars; stand firm, Pandavas.
mahabharata:9:31.18	Today I shall be quit of my debt to the glorious kshatriyas—Bahlika, Drona, Bhishma, and the great-souled Karna,
mahabharata:9:31.19	the hero Jayadratha, both Bhagadatta and Bhurishravas, Shalya the king of the Madras,
mahabharata:9:31.20	my sons, O best of the Bharatas, Shakuni son of Subala, and my friends, well-wishers and kinsmen.
mahabharata:9:31.21	Today I shall be free of the debt, having slain you with your brothers. Having said this much, the lord of men fell silent.
[Yudhishthira said:] "By good fortune you too know a kshatriya's duty, Suyodhana; by good fortune your mind is set on battle, mighty-armed one.
By good fortune you are a hero, Kaurava; by good fortune you know war, who alone wish to fight us all in the battle.
Meeting one by one, take whatever weapon you approve and fight; we stand as spectators.
And I give you this further wish, hero: having slain one of us, take the kingdom, or, slain, gain heaven."
[Duryodhana said:] "If a boon is given me today to fight one in the contest, then of weapons I choose this mace, with your approval.
Whichever one of you brothers thinks he can face me, let him fight me on foot with a mace in the battle.
Chariot-fights, varied at every step, have been fought; let this one mace-fight be great and wondrous today.
Men wish to change even their foods in turn; with your approval let there be a change of battles too.
With the mace, mighty-armed one, I shall conquer you with your younger brothers, the Panchalas, the Srinjayas and all your other soldiers."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Rise, rise, Gandhari's son; fight me, Suyodhana, meeting one against one in battle with the mace, mighty one.
Be a man, son of Gandhari, and fight with full attention; today you have no life, even if you are swift as thought."
[Sanjaya said:] Your son, tiger among men, could not bear this, lying in the water, hissing like a great serpent in a pit.
Goaded again and again by that whip of words, the wise one could not endure the speech, like a fine horse the lash.
Churning the water with force, the mighty one took up his heavy iron mace adorned with golden armlets and rose from within the water, hissing like a king of serpents.
Having split the stilled water, he rose with the iron mace on his shoulder, your son, blazing like the radiant sun.
Then the wise, mighty son of Dhritarashtra grasped his heavy mace of iron and gold, adorned with gold.
Seeing him mace in hand, like a mountain with peaks, like Shiva enraged at creatures, trident in hand, the Bharata with his mace shone like the blazing sun.
Seeing him risen, mace in hand, the mighty-armed subduer of foes, all beings thought him like Death with staff in hand.
All the Panchalas saw your son, lord of men, like Shakra with the thunderbolt in hand, or Hara with the trident.
Seeing him risen, the Panchalas and Pandavas were all delighted and clapped their hands to one another.
Taking that for derision, your son Duryodhana, rolling his eyes in anger as if to burn the Pandavas,
knitting his brow in three lines, biting his lip, replied to the Pandavas along with Keshava:
For this derision of yours today I shall answer, Pandavas; you shall go at once, slain with your Panchalas, to Yama's abode.
Risen from that water, your son Duryodhana stood, mace in hand, drenched in blood.
Smeared with blood and water, his body then shone like a mountain with streams flowing.
The Pandavas there thought the hero with raised mace like enraged Vaivasvata (Yama) with his servants' hands raised.
With a voice like thunder, bellowing with joy like a bull, the mighty one then challenged the Parthas to a mace-fight.
[Duryodhana said:] "Approach me one at a time, Yudhishthira; it is not proper, hero, for one to fight many in battle,
especially one with armour laid aside, weary, wading in water, with limbs sorely wounded, his mounts and soldiers slain."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Where was this wisdom of yours, Suyodhana, when many great chariot-warriors slew Abhimanyu in battle?
Put on armour, hero, and tie your hair, and take whatever else you lack, Bharata; and I give you this further wish, hero:
of the five Pandavas, whomever you wish to fight here, having slain him you may be king, or slain, gain heaven. Except for your life, hero, what more can we do for you in the battle?"
[Sanjaya said:] Then your son, O king, took up golden armour and a splendid helmet adorned with Jambunada gold.
With helmet bound and wearing fine golden armour, your son shone, O king, like a golden king of mountains.
Armoured, mace in hand, O king, ready at the head of the battle, your son Duryodhana said to all the Pandavas:

Of you brothers, let one fight me with the mace—I shall fight Sahadeva, or Bhima, or Nakula,
mahabharata:9:31.58	or Phalguna today, or you, bull of the Bharatas; I shall fight, entering the contest, and conquer in the battle.
mahabharata:9:31.59	Today I shall reach the end of the enmity, hard to reach, with my mace bound with gold bands, tiger among men.
mahabharata:9:31.60	Think that none is my equal in mace-fighting; with the mace I shall slay all of you assembled. Let whoever will fight me today take his mace.
[Vasudeva said:] "If he were to choose you, Yudhishthira, or Arjuna, or Nakula, or even Sahadeva,
what is this rashness, O king, that you have uttered—'Slaying just one in the battle, become king'?
For thirteen years this man has trained on an iron figure, wishing to slay Bhimasena.
How shall we proceed, bull of the Bharatas? You, best of kings, have done a rash thing out of compassion.
I see no other opponent for him in battle except Vrikodara or Partha, and the latter has not trained greatly.
This is the same gamble begun again as before, uneven, between Shakuni and you, lord of men.
Bhima is strong and capable, but King Suyodhana is skilled; between the strong and the skilled, O king, the skilled is the better.
You have set this enemy, Rama's delight, on level ground and placed ourselves in a very uneven spot; we have fallen into difficulty.
Who, having conquered all enemies, would wager everything on a single stake against one foe and so relish such a fight?
I see no one in the world, mace in hand, best of men, who could fight Duryodhana in battle and surpass him in skill.
Neither Phalguna, nor you, nor the sons of Madri—I do not think any of them equal to him in battle with the mace in hand.
How then do you say to the enemy, 'Fight with the mace—slay just one of us and be king,' Bharata?
Having come to Vrikodara, our victory is in doubt; fighting fairly, this mighty one is skilled."
[Bhima said:] "Madhusudana, do not despair, delight of the Yadus; today I shall reach the end of this very hard-to-cross enmity.
I shall slay Suyodhana in the battle, without doubt; victory, Krishna, is surely seen for the king of dharma.
My mace is heavier by half than his; do not be troubled, Madhava.
I could fight in battle, delighted, the three worlds with the gods, bearing various weapons; how much more Suyodhana today!"
[Sanjaya said:] As Vrikodara spoke thus, Vasudeva, pleased, honoured him and spoke these words.

Relying on you, mighty-armed one, Dharmaraja Yudhishthira, his enemies slain, has gained his own blazing fortune, without doubt.
mahabharata:9:32.21	By you all the sons of Dhritarashtra have been slain in battle, and kings, princes and elephants felled.
mahabharata:9:32.22	The Kalingas, Magadhas, Easterners, Gandharas and Kurus, meeting you in the great war, were slain, son of Pandu.
mahabharata:9:32.23	Having slain Duryodhana too, give the earth with her oceans to Dharmaraja, son of Kunti, as Vishnu gave it to the lord of Shachi.
mahabharata:9:32.24	Meeting you in battle, the sinful son of Dhritarashtra will perish; you will fulfil your vow by breaking his thighs.
mahabharata:9:32.25	Yet, Partha, the son of Dhritarashtra must always be fought with care, for he is skilled, strong and ever proud in battle.
Then Satyaki, O king, honoured the Pandava, and Madhava honoured him with various words.
The Panchalas and Pandavas, with Dharmaraja at their head, all honoured those words of Bhimasena.
Then terrible Bhima of terrible strength said to Yudhishthira, who stood with the Srinjayas, blazing like the sun:

Meeting him in battle I am able to fight; this vilest of men cannot conquer me in the fight.
mahabharata:9:32.30	Today I shall release the anger long stored in my heart against Suyodhana, Dhritarashtra's son, as Arjuna released fire upon Khandava.
mahabharata:9:32.31	Today I shall pull out the dart in your heart, Pandava; having slain the sinful one with my mace, be happy today, O king.
mahabharata:9:32.32	Today, blameless one, I shall put on you the garland of fame; today Suyodhana will lose life, fortune and kingdom.
mahabharata:9:32.33	And King Dhritarashtra today, hearing his son slain by me, will remember the evil deed born of Shakuni's counsel.
While those crows slept confidently on every side, he saw an owl of dreadful aspect suddenly approaching.
These sparks, indeed, burn men; cast off anger with wisdom and steady yourself by yourself.
Nor was Pritha's secret, or his, ever laid open, sage; then that mighty archer hero was felled by Partha.
Or if this is your view, that they too impel one another, then doubt arises about cause and effect through mutual prompting.
The duties of kshatriyas, whose livelihood is war, are known to you; a king acting according to his course is not bound by any fetter.
Thus Yudhishthira, king of dharma, best of the upholders of dharma, the wise one, with his brothers, honoured that king.
They also scorned their elders, though not Rama and Janardana; wives were unfaithful to husbands, and husbands to wives.
This Phalguna, your brother, should abandon the Gandiva, the supreme weapon, and go to the forest; it is of no use to him.
What use is heaven to me, O best of gods, bereft of my brothers? Wherever they are, that is heaven to me; this is not heaven in my view.
